C005.subject: Raising the minimum wage in high-productivity urban markets
C005.object: by reducing turnover costs more than it increases labor costs, due to lower voluntary quits
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Raising the minimum wage in high-productivity urban markets by reducing turnover costs more than it increases labor costs, due to lower voluntary quits]

[PATH:empirical] Quasi-experimental studies of minimum wage increases in high-productivity U.S. cities (e.g., Seattle, San Francisco) using synthetic control methods to estimate effects on turnover and net profits — Directly tests the net profitability effect by comparing treated urban markets to matched controls, isolating turnover cost reductions from labor cost increases.

[PATH:empirical] Firm-level panel data analysis from high-productivity sectors (e.g., tech, finance) linking wage floors to employee quit rates and hiring costs, using administrative payroll and turnover records — Provides micro-level evidence on the causal chain: higher minimum wage → lower voluntary quits → reduced turnover costs, enabling calculation of net profit impact.

[PATH:theoretical] Monopsony labor market models incorporating firm-specific turnover cost functions and wage-setting power, calibrated to urban labor markets — Formalizes the conditions under which turnover cost savings outweigh wage increases, predicting thresholds for net profitability gains and identifying boundary conditions.

qualifier.geographic: high-productivity urban markets in developed economies

C006.subject: Raising the minimum wage in high-productivity urban markets
C006.object: by incentivizing employers to automate jobs or relocate to lower-cost areas
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Raising the minimum wage in high-productivity urban markets by incentivizing employers to automate jobs or relocate to lower-cost areas]

[PATH:empirical] Difference-in-differences analysis of minimum wage increases in high-productivity U.S. cities (e.g., Seattle, San Francisco, New York) using county-level employment and automation adoption data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics and the Annual Survey of Manufactures — Directly tests whether minimum wage hikes correlate with increased automation (e.g., robot density per worker) or net job losses due to relocation, controlling for local productivity trends and other confounding factors.

[PATH:empirical] Survey or case study evidence from employer decision-making in high-productivity urban service and manufacturing sectors (e.g., retail, logistics, food service) on substitution of labor with capital or relocation to lower-cost regions — Provides micro-level behavioral data to assess whether turnover cost increases are a primary mechanism driving automation or relocation, complementing aggregate econometric findings.

[PATH:theoretical] Acemoglu and Restrepo (2019) 'Automation and New Tasks: How Technology Displaces and Reinstates Labor' and related literature on the elasticity of substitution between labor and capital in response to wage shocks — Offers a theoretical framework predicting that minimum wage hikes raise the relative cost of low-skill labor, incentivizing automation, especially in high-productivity urban markets where capital is more accessible; this can be used to derive testable predictions and calibrate models.

qualifier.temporal: post-2000, during periods of rising minimum wage legislation in U.S. cities
qualifier.geographic: high-productivity urban markets in the United States

C007.subject: Raising the minimum wage in high-productivity urban markets under tight labor supply
C007.object: when firms can partially automate low-skill tasks instead of retaining or upskilling workers
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Raising the minimum wage in high-productivity urban markets under tight labor supply when firms can partially automate low-skill tasks instead of retaining or upskilling workers]

[PATH:empirical] Firm-level panel data from high-productivity urban markets (e.g., U.S. metro areas with tight labor markets) tracking changes in minimum wage, automation adoption, and training expenditures over time — Directly tests the causal effect of minimum wage increases on firm training investment, controlling for automation adoption, using difference-in-differences or event-study methods.

[PATH:empirical] Survey or experimental study of firm managers in high-productivity urban markets, eliciting substitution intentions between training and automation under hypothetical minimum wage increases — Provides behavioral micro-foundations for the substitution mechanism, revealing whether firms perceive automation as a viable alternative to upskilling when labor costs rise.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical models of firm training and automation decisions under labor market tightness and wage floors (e.g., Acemoglu & Restrepo 2018, or related search/matching models) — Establishes formal conditions under which minimum wage hikes reduce training incentives, and identifies countervailing forces (e.g., complementarity between skilled labor and automation) that could refute the hypothesis.

scope.domain: firm behavior, automation, labor market tightness

qualifier.temporal: during periods of tight labor supply and ongoing automation adoption

C008.subject: Raising the minimum wage in high-productivity urban markets
C008.object: even when labor supply is not tight because firms aim to enhance worker productivity and retain talent
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Raising the minimum wage in high-productivity urban markets even when labor supply is not tight because firms aim to enhance worker productivity and retain talent]

[PATH:empirical] Panel data on firm-level training expenditures and minimum wage changes in U.S. metropolitan areas (e.g., from the Bureau of Labor Statistics or matched employer-employee datasets like LEHD) — Directly tests whether firms increase training investment following minimum wage hikes in high-productivity urban markets with slack labor supply, using difference-in-differences or event-study designs.

[PATH:empirical] Survey or case study evidence from firms in high-productivity urban sectors (e.g., tech, finance, advanced services) on their human capital investment decisions post minimum wage increases — Qualitative and quantitative micro-level data can reveal whether firms explicitly cite productivity enhancement and retention motives for training when labor supply is slack, providing causal mechanism evidence.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical models of efficiency wage and human capital investment under wage floors (e.g., Acemoglu & Pischke, 1999; recent extensions with labor market frictions) — Formal models can clarify conditions under which minimum wage increases incentivize firm-sponsored training even without tight labor supply, helping to refine the hypothesis and identify testable predictions.

qualifier.temporal: post-2010, during periods of moderate labor market slack
qualifier.geographic: high-productivity urban markets in developed economies

C011.predicate: accelerates the displacement of low-skill workers into informal or gig employment

evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Raising the minimum wage in high-productivity urban markets because firms facing thin profit margins prioritize automation and reduce formal low-skill positions, pushing workers into less stable work arrangements]

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal employer-employee matched datasets from cities like San Francisco, Seattle, or New York, tracking firm-level automation investments and low-skill employment transitions before and after minimum wage increases. — Directly tests whether firms in thin-margin sectors (e.g., retail, food service) substitute capital for labor following wage hikes, and whether displaced workers enter gig or informal work, using causal identification strategies like difference-in-differences.

[PATH:empirical] Survey and administrative data on gig economy participation (e.g., Uber, TaskRabbit, or IRS 1099 records) linked to local minimum wage ordinances, analyzed with spatial or temporal variation. — Provides evidence on the displacement channel by measuring shifts from formal employment to platform-mediated or informal work in high-cost urban markets, controlling for local labor demand shocks.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical models of labor market dualism with endogenous automation (e.g., Acemoglu & Restrepo 2018, or task-based frameworks) calibrated to high-productivity urban economies. — Explores the causal mechanism—firms' profit-maximizing response to wage floors—and generates testable predictions about the elasticity of substitution between low-skill labor and automation under thin margins.

qualifier.temporal: post-2000, during periods of rising minimum wage adjustments in high-cost urban labor markets
qualifier.geographic: high-productivity urban markets in developed economies, e.g., major cities in the United States and Western Europe
